slides.headline: Why your glutes deserve more attention
slides.sub: The Pilates approach: control first, then load.

slides.title: More than looks
slides.body: Your glutes help control your hips and knees when you walk, run, climb stairs and lift. Stronger glutes can make everyday movement feel more solid and less effortful.

slides.title: Start with control
slides.body: Pilates begins by feeling the right muscles work. A slow bridge, peeling the spine up and down, teaches you to use your glutes rather than arching through your lower back.

slides.title: Work the side of the hip
slides.body: Side-lying leg lifts, clams and standing leg work on the reformer target the muscles on the side of the hip that steady your pelvis when you stand on one leg.

slides.title: Then add load
slides.body: Springs, bands and single-leg work progress the challenge. Muscles get stronger when the effort increases gradually, so your program should build up over the weeks.

slides.title: A quick home trio
slides.body: Try ten slow bridges, ten clams each side and a thirty-second single-leg balance on each side. Two or three times a week is a good starting point.

slides.headline: Build glutes that support you
slides.body: Our Pilates team assesses how you move and progresses your program as you get stronger. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Your glutes do a lot more than fill out your jeans.

They help control your hips and knees every time you walk, run, climb stairs or lift something. The Pilates approach starts with control, learning to feel the right muscles work in a slow bridge or clam, then gradually adds load with springs, bands and single-leg work.

Want to start today? Try ten slow bridges, ten clams each side and a thirty-second single-leg balance, two or three times a week.
